analysis.one_liner: Keeps the 3.4% student loan interest rate for one more year, paid for by new payroll taxes on high-earning professionals.
analysis.headline: 51 senators backed extending the 3.4% student loan rate, but the bill failed 51-43 on May 24, 2012, because 60 votes were required and not a single Republican supported it in either vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Subsidized federal student loans for undergraduates carried a 3.4% interest rate that was scheduled to double back to the standard 6.8% on July 1, 2012. This bill would have extended the 3.4% rate for one more year. To cover the cost, it would have required partners and shareholders in professional service businesses—law, medicine, lobbying, consulting, accounting, investment advice, and similar fields—earning more than $200,000 a year ($250,000 for joint filers) to pay self-employment payroll tax on their business income, which they currently avoid. Senate Republicans blocked the bill from debate, and it failed on the one vote the chamber allowed.
analysis.who_benefits: Undergraduate students borrowing subsidized federal Stafford loans, who would keep the 3.4% rate for loans issued through July 1, 2013 instead of paying 6.8% — roughly double the interest over the life of each loan.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the 3.4% interest rate on Direct Stafford loans first disbursed to undergraduates through July 1, 2013, rather than letting it expire after July 1, 2012.
The rate cut applies automatically to new loans; borrowers do not have to apply for anything.

analysis.who_pays: Partners and shareholders in professional service businesses earning more than $200,000 a year ($250,000 for couples) would begin paying self-employment payroll tax on their share of business income — income that is currently exempt when earned through an S corporation or partnership.

drawbacks.text: The fix lasts only one year: the bill extends the reduced rate through loans disbursed before July 1, 2013, so the rate question would return immediately, as it did in earlier short-term extensions.

The pay-for is a targeted tax increase on a specific group: partners and shareholders in law firms, medical practices, lobbying shops, consulting and accounting firms, and investment businesses above the $200,000/$250,000 income thresholds would owe payroll tax on pass-through income they currently avoid.
The new tax reaches family members who hold shares but do not work in the business, treating the shareholder's pro-rata share as earned income — a broad sweep beyond just working owners.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is clear and large: millions of undergraduate borrowers avoid a doubling of their loan rate for one year, funded by a payroll tax on high-income professionals in specific service fields. The tax only touches people above $200,000 in income, so the cost lands on a small, affluent group, but the bill's one-year sunset means it postpones rather than settles the underlying rate dispute. An honest supporter would acknowledge both that the pay-for draws objections from affected professionals and that a single-year patch was the design both parties had already been living with.

outcome.mechanism: Republicans blocked the motion to begin debate, and when the Senate finally took a vote under an order requiring 60 votes to pass, the bill failed 51-43 with all voting Democrats in favor and no Republicans; it never got an ordinary up-or-down vote.

narrative.text: Senator Harry Reid introduced the bill on April 24, 2012, and it was placed directly on the Senate calendar.

On May 8, 2012, the Senate voted 52-45 on whether to open debate — a vote that needed 60 because of the filibuster rule — and it failed; every Republican who voted was opposed, while 50 of 51 Democrats and the independent supported it.

On May 24, 2012, the motion to proceed was agreed to by unanimous consent, and the Senate then voted 51-43 under a prior order requiring 60 votes for passage; 49 of 51 Democrats supported the bill and 42 of 47 Republicans opposed it.
The bill was returned to the calendar and the Congress ended in January 2013 without it ever being enacted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-earning partners and shareholders in professional service firms kept paying no payroll tax on their business income, and the reduced student loan rate was left to expire on schedule in July 2012 — borrowers bore the doubled rate instead.

for.name: Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, placed it on the calendar, and repeatedly moved to bring it to the floor, including filing a cloture motion after debate was blocked.

for.name: 49 of 51 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted for the bill on the May 24 passage vote; one week earlier, all but one Democrat had voted to open debate.

for.name: President Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned that spring for Congress to stop the scheduled doubling of the student loan rate before the July 1 deadline.

against.name: 44 of 47 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against the motion to open debate on May 8 and against passage on May 24; no Republican voted for the bill in either vote.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Led the Republican opposition, arguing the bill's pay-for was a tax increase on small businesses organized as S corporations and partnerships.

sides.party_line_note: The split was total: 50 of 51 Democrats and the one independent voted to open debate and 49 of 51 voted for passage, while zero of the 44 Republicans voting in the first vote and zero of the 42 voting in the second ever supported the bill.

industries.industry: Professional service firms (law, lobbying, medicine, consulting, accounting, actuarial, investment advice and brokerage)
industries.note: Partners and shareholders earning over $200,000 ($250,000 joint) would have begun paying self-employment payroll tax on their share of business income — money that funds the student rate extension. Their interest in stopping the bill ran directly against borrowers' interest in keeping the lower rate.
